premise: The reference audit found that the biological and computational literatures in this project never once talk about the same object. This runs the computational thesis's own hypothesis on a real biological graph, against a null that has the same degree sequence and none of the biology.
hypothesis: Reordering that respects biological community structure should improve memory locality MORE on a real biological graph than on a random graph with the identical degree sequence. The weak form of this claim is untestable; this is the strong form, and it is allowed to come back negative.

nullFidelity.note: The configuration model produces parallel edges and self-loops; collapsing them loses a few. Reported because a null that quietly differs in size is not a null.

finding: Community-aware reordering cuts cache lines per row by 51.7% on the real graph and 2.5% on the degree-matched null — an excess of 49.2 percentage points that the degree sequence alone does not explain. The real graph carries modularity 0.861 against 0.162 for the rewiring, which is where the excess comes from. SpMV wall clock moves too — 0.187 ms down to 0.124 ms, about 34% — so this is a locality gain and not only a locality metric. And the half that does not flatter the hypothesis: reverse Cuthill-McKee, which knows nothing about biology, cuts cache lines by 67.3%, MORE than the community ordering does. Biological structure is exploitable; exploiting it through communities is not yet better than a bandwidth heuristic from 1969. One graph, one metric, one machine.

versusClassical.says: Community-aware ordering cuts cache lines by 51.7%. Reverse Cuthill-McKee, which knows nothing about biology and predates the field, cuts them by 67.3%. The classical ordering WINS. Biological structure is demonstrably exploitable — the null says so by fifty points — and exploiting it through communities is not yet better than a bandwidth heuristic from 1969. That is the author's own recorded caution about assuming community reorganisation beats a tuned general method, holding, on the first graph anyone measured.
